title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) is an advanced wound care modality that enhances healing through the application of controlled subatmospheric pressure to reduce exudate and promote granulation tissue formation. This article explains the mechanisms of NPWT, reviews its indications and contraindications, discusses emerging and evolving applications in modern wound care, and presents practical approaches to implementation. This activity also reviews the historical evolution of NPWT, its core mechanisms of action, device components, and expanding clinical indications across acute, chronic, and closed surgical wounds.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Emphasis is placed on the importance of appropriate wound debridement, dressing selection, creation of an airtight seal, and individualized pressure settings to ensure safe and effective therapy. This activity also provides practical guidance on traditional vacuum-assisted closure systems, disposable and portable devices, and emerging techniques such as NPWT with instillation. In addition, this activity emphasizes the roles and responsibilities of the interdisciplinary healthcare team, the importance of effective collaboration, and the training and expertise required to optimize NPWT application and improve patient outcomes. Recognizing that indications vary by clinical context, the activity also outlines appropriate use of NPWT and supports sound clinical judgment in the management of complex wounds to achieve high-quality clinical outcomes in a healthcare setting.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify appropriate indications and contraindications for negative pressure wound therapy across acute, chronic, and closed surgical wounds. Implement negative pressure wound therapy using proper wound preparation, debridement, dressing placement, and airtight sealing techniques. Select adjunctive measures, such as interface dressings, protective barriers, or instillation solutions, to optimize wound healing and patient comfort. Collaborate with interdisciplinary healthcare team members to coordinate wound care, dressing changes, and ongoing treatment planning. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Introduction
content: Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) is a unique and versatile wound care system that optimizes wound healing by applying subatmospheric pressure through specialized wound dressings. This approach reduces inflammatory exudate and promotes the formation of granulation tissue. NPWT has evolved since early systems were first introduced in the 19th century. [1] The modern standard NPWT was described by Argenta and Morykwas in 1997 and consists of a porous foam dressing to which continuous or intermittent suction is applied, which can be set to a pressure up to 125 mm Hg. [2] NPWT, also referred to as vacuum-assisted closure (VAC), is effective for both acute and chronic wounds, and is frequently applied to open wounds, including fractures, ulcers, and infected wounds, as well as open surgical wounds. More recently, NPWT been applied to include new closed surgical wounds and skin grafts. [3]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Introduction
content: NPWT reduces edema and seroma formation, promotes granulation tissue formation, and is believed to decrease the risk of surgical wound dehiscence in high-risk sites. Although the evidence supporting the use of NPWT in closed incisions remains equivocal, its use has increased across various clinical settings, including complex arthroplasty and wounds at high risk of dehiscence or infection. Specifically, this practice has been associated with reductions in infection sites, morbidity, and mortality among those undergoing vascular surgery procedures. [4] [5] [6] NPWT has also been shown to reduce wound infections and dehiscence rates in patients undergoing vulvar surgery. [7]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Introduction
content: The wound dressing system can be placed in the operating room, at the bedside, or in an examination room. Pressure settings are tailored to different types of wounds. The foam dressing is derived from either polyurethane (black) or polyvinyl alcohol (white) and can be silver impregnated. Disposable systems, whether battery-operated or mechanical suction-only, are typically used for smaller wounds in ambulatory patients. [8] Negative pressure systems may also be used in conjunction with saline or antibiotic instillation into wounds to enhance the delivery of these therapies to the wound beds. [9]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The skin is a laminated structure composed of the epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis, the latter also referred to as the subcutaneous or fatty tissue layer. The epidermis is further subdivided into the stratum corneum, stratum lucidum, stratum granulosum, stratum spinosum, and stratum basale. Each of these layers has a unique structure, cellular composition, and function within the epidermis. This microscopic infrastructure contributes to the macroscopic processes that maintain skin integrity, including wound healing. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Anatomy, Skin (Integument), Epidermis ," for more information.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Wound healing is broadly categorized into acute and chronic phases. Following an acute skin injury, a proinflammatory cascade is initiated that promotes hemostasis and triggers the release of inflammatory mediators, including neutrophils and cytokines, typically within the first 7 days after injury. The inflammatory phase is followed by the proliferative and re-epithelialization phases, which involve endothelial cells and fibroblasts and support angiogenesis and innervation. Together, these processes lead to the formation of healthy granulation tissue. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Wound Healing Phases ," for more information.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: As granulation tissue begins to form, wound healing progresses into the remodeling phase, during which epithelial restoration occurs and tissue strength is gradually reestablished. This phase may last between 12 and 24 months. Remodeling is mediated by growth factors, including fibroblast growth factor and epidermal growth factor, which support collagen deposition and the formation of a cross-linked extracellular matrix. [10] [11]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: A chronic wound is an open wound that fails to progress through the normal stages of healing within an expected time frame. A hallmark feature of chronic wounds is prolonged stasis in the inflammatory phase, reflecting dysregulation of normal healing processes. Common etiologies include repetitive tissue stress and a persistent inflammatory trigger such as microbial infection. [12] Diabetic ulcers and wounds associated with vascular insufficiency or neuropathy exhibit impaired immune responses and a local environment that favors chronicity. In these wounds, tissue perfusion is reduced and levels of inflammatory mediators are elevated, increasing the risk of infection and further impairing healing mechanisms. [13]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The pathophysiology of chronic wounds involves protease-induced degradation of the extracellular matrix, persistent infiltration of proinflammatory cytokines, and attenuated growth factor signaling. This, in combination with biofilm deposition and excessive fibrous tissue, such as collagen and fibronectin, ultimately creates a proinflammatory cycle that impedes progression to the proliferative phase. The cardinal microscopic findings in chronic wound tissue are macrophages, excessive granulation tissue, and fibrosis. Eventually, these mediators promote excessive scar formation and poor skin compliance. [13]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: NPWT optimizes wound-healing physiology through both macro- and micro-mechanical effects generated by the application of negative pressure. Wound deformation refers to wound contraction at both the gross and microscopic tissue levels. Mechanical pressure stimulates a cellular signaling cascade that leads to excess fluid removal and progression of the wound microenvironment toward healing. Negative pressure induces wound contraction. Macrodeformation has been reported to reduce the wound area by approximately 80%. Suction generated through the pores of the foam dressing produces microdeformation, which generates mechanical stress on the wound surface and causes microscopic ripples to form along the edges of the wound due to increased tissue tension. These deformation mechanisms promote physiological cellular proliferation, migration, differentiation, and angiogenesis, in part through hypoxia-induced release of vascular endothelial growth factors. In addition, negative pressure actively removes excess inflammatory exudate from the wound site, helping to restore microvascular circulation. Removing excess extracellular fluid reestablishes normal oncotic and osmotic pressure gradients and promotes endothelial, epithelial, and keratinocyte cell migration. [14]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Indications
content: NPWT is used to treat complex or deep wounds that are nonhealing, at risk of delayed healing, or likely to benefit from accelerated healing via negative pressure. NPWT is indicated for both acute and chronic wounds and is often used for acute wounds that cannot be closed by primary intention due to insufficient epidermal coverage, risk of infection, active infection, or excessive skin tension resulting from edema or other causes. [15]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Indications
content: Acute wounds treated with NPWT include open fractures and lacerations, some partial-thickness degloving injuries and burns, and surgical wounds resulting from contaminated surgery or debridements of necrotizing infections or compartment syndromes. Immediate primary closure or skin grafting of many of these wounds would trap devitalized tissue and microorganisms within the soft tissue, leading to abscesses and dehiscence.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Indications
content: NPWT is also used for acute or chronic dehisced wounds, which are often refractory to primary closure. In these cases, negative pressure therapy may serve as an intermediate treatment by promoting granulation tissue formation and wound edge contraction, thereby facilitating successful closure. Similarly, NPWT can be used to prepare a healthy wound bed to enhance skin graft uptake. Additional indications for NPWT include use as a bolster for closed wounds, such as skin flaps and grafts. [16] NPWT has also been shown to be an effective adjunct to compression therapy in the treatment of nonhealing venous leg ulcers, reducing healing time compared with compression alone. [17] [18]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Contraindications
content: A thorough wound assessment must be carried out before initiating NPWT. Any exposed vasculature, bowel, or other intra-abdominal or vulnerable structures should be identified. When NPWT is used in wounds with exposed anatomy that could be injured by negative pressure, dressing materials and pressure settings should be modified accordingly. For example, protective intervening dressings may be placed between the foam and bowel, and lower pressure settings may be selected. Applying NPWT directly over a fistula may result in excessive fluid extraction or tissue injury, potentially leading to dehydration and damage to adjacent vital structures. [14]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Contraindications
content: All necrotic or devitalized tissue should be adequately debrided, and active infection treated before NPWT application. Although case reports have described the use of NPWT in wound beds with active osteomyelitis without adverse outcomes, this approach is not considered standard of care. [19] The presence of an underlying malignancy is also considered a contraindication to NPWT due to the theoretical risk of tumor seeding. [20]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Equipment
content: The following describes equipment for the placement of an NPWT system. Additional supplies may be necessary for any indicated soft tissue debridement or procedures performed in an operative setting before dressing placement. NWPT is typically a nonsterile procedure, although it may be placed using sterile technique when clinically indicated. A negative pressure dressing set consists of: Foam or gauze dressings that are available in a variety of sizes Transparent, double-sided adhesive drapes arranged in sequential layering Suction tubing attached to a suction disk placed on top of the foam A suction device that is either battery-operated or powered by an electrical outlet A collection canister for wound exudate

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Personnel
content: Many healthcare providers are trained to apply negative pressure dressings, including physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and bedside nurses. Initial dressing placement is often performed by the clinician primarily responsible for wound management, while subsequent dressing changes may be carried out by additional trained staff according to documented care instructions. The wound etiology and the patient’s overall clinical status guide the frequency of dressing changes and the need for adjunctive measures, such as irrigation or sedation. When NPWT is applied over a skin graft or other closed wound, the dressing may remain in place until postoperative inspection by the operating surgeon. In complex trauma cases, including those involving an open abdomen or necrotizing infections, intensive care personnel may also be involved in wound management.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Preparation
content: The efficacy of NPWT relies on a thorough debridement and irrigation of the wound to promote healthy granulation tissue and encourage wound apposition. Initial placement may occur in the operating room following surgical intervention or at the bedside. If not previously obtained, informed consent should be secured from the patient or family prior to application. [21]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Preparation
content: The patient is positioned to allow optimal access to the wound. When indicated, medications may be administered to ensure patient comfort during the procedure. The wound is cleared of nonviable tissue and gently irrigated with normal saline or an appropriate antiseptic solution, such as chlorhexidine or a related agent. After wound bed preparation, the area is dried with sterile gauze, and the surrounding skin is cleansed and dried. A skin preparation product may be applied to protect the skin from abrasive trauma. If a prior NWPT dressing is in place, adhesive remover may be gently applied to help lift the dressing from the skin to avoid trauma and minimize skin injury. [22]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Technique or Treatment
content: The patient is positioned to ensure full access to the wound, and the wound and surrounding skin are cleansed and prepared. All nonviable tissue is sharply debrided using sterile forceps, scissors, or a scalpel. Active bleeding is controlled with electrocautery or direct pressure until hemostasis is achieved. The foam dressing is then trimmed by hand to match the exact dimensions of the wound and placed to ensure contact with all areas of dead space. Any undermined areas should be loosely packed with foam. When possible, the wound should be covered with a single piece of foam to maintain continuity; however, multiple pieces may be used for large or irregular wounds. The total number of foam pieces placed must be documented to prevent inadvertent retention within the wound bed.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Technique or Treatment
content: Once the wound is fully covered with foam, the wound bed and a circumference of surrounding skin are sealed with transparent adhesive sealant tape to create a secure, airtight seal around the foam dressing. The adhesive sheets included in NPWT kits are designed for sequential removal of the backing, allowing precise contact of the central portion of each sheet onto the wound before removing the covering of the adhesive on the edges. This design helps prevent unintended adherence of the adhesive to itself, surrounding objects, or personnel during application. The adhesive tapes should be applied to eliminate all potential air gaps.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Technique or Treatment
content: The next step involves connecting the suction tubing to the foam dressing. Depending on the VAC system used, the suction tubing may be positioned directly over the foam dressing before applying the transparent adhesive sealant tape or incorporated into a separate adhesive dressing placed on top of the transparent adhesive sealant tape. In most kits, the wound end of the tubing is attached using an adhesive disk positioned over the central portion of the foam. A couple of discrete holes are created in the adhesive sheet beneath the disk to allow communication between the foam and the suction apparatus, after which the disk is secured in place. The suction tubing is then connected to the apparatus containing the suction motor and collection canister. The device is set to the prescribed negative pressure and activated after inspection, thereby confirming that the tubing is unobstructed and not clamped or kinked. [23]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Technique or Treatment
content: Upon initial activation of suction, the dressing should be closely inspected. When functioning properly, the sponge rapidly and homogenously compresses under negative pressure, and the device operates without air-leak alarms, often indicated by a steady green light and an audible motor hum. If an air-leak alarm occurs, additional adhesive tape should be applied to seal any gaps. When multiple wound areas require treatment and are separated by intact skin, a foam bridge may be constructed to maintain continuity of the dressing. The underlying intact skin should be protected with a barrier such as Tegaderm or a transparent film dressing, and foam is placed over this surface. Less commonly, a Y-connector may be used if available in the system. When NPWT is applied to closed wounds, the incision is first protected with an appropriate dressing and then covered with an adhesive drape with reinforced edges to ensure a secure, airtight seal. [23]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Technique or Treatment
content: All active NPWT systems should be routinely monitored for proper function and for the volume and characteristics of wound drainage. If the device alarms, the dressing seal may require reinforcement with additional adhesive, or the dressing may need to be replaced. Loss of negative pressure in heavily exudative wounds can result in uncontrolled drainage that saturates the wound, dressing, and surrounding skin; prompt cleansing is necessary to prevent skin breakdown and support ongoing healing. Throughout NPWT treatment, nutritional status and comorbid conditions should be closely monitored, as they can significantly affect wound healing outcomes. [18]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Complications
content: The most common complications associated with NPWT include pain, bleeding, infection, and inadvertent retention of foam dressing, which can lead to infection. A common mechanical complication is ineffective therapy delivery due to loss of suction, most frequently caused by an inadequate seal around the dressing. This should be remedied as soon as it is detected to avoid any disruption in negative pressure therapy. Other causes of therapy failure include improper suction tube placement, tube blockage, loss of battery power, or a full cannister. [24]

Other causes of therapy failure include improper suction tube placement, tube blockage, loss of battery power, or a full cannister. [24]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Complications
content: Other complications include hypersensitivity reactions to dressing materials or maceration due to excessive moisture. Additional damage to the wound may occur, including erosion or necrosis, as well as damage to underlying structures such as blood vessels or bowel, including recent anastomoses. If skin breakdown or localized pain develops around the site of negative pressure application, topical emollient therapy may be used, or an alternative nonadherent dressing can be placed under the transparent adhesive sealant tape. Regular wound assessment should include examination for any discoloration, duskiness, or mottling of the wound bed or wound edges. [25] Ongoing monitoring of hydration status is also important, with intravenous maintenance fluids administered as needed. [14]

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Clinical Significance
content: When applied correctly by trained healthcare professionals, NPWT is an effective therapy for the management of open and complex wounds, leading to faster wound healing, reduced discomfort, and improved functional outcomes for affected patients. NPWT has broad clinical applicability across multiple specialties, including, but not limited to, vascular, orthopedic, trauma, and plastic surgery. The type of wounds involved and the overall clinical status of patients determine the duration and therapeutic goals of NPWT. By facilitating wound stabilization and mobility, NPWT can improve the quality of life for patients with significant wounds during the healing process. [14]

content: NPWT is a cornerstone of advanced wound care and is highly effective in managing complex acute and chronic wounds. [14] Optimal outcomes depend on the correct application of dressing by appropriately trained personnel. Healthcare professionals who use NPWT should receive formal training and maintain familiarity with the relevant anatomy, physiology, indications, and contraindications associated with this this wound care modality.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: One of the key advantages of NPWT is that it can be implemented and managed by multiple members of the interprofessional healthcare team, including physicians, nurses, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants. Effective NPWT care requires a collaborative approach, with routine assessment of the wound, monitoring of system function and drainage, and timely performance of scheduled or clinically indicated dressing changes. NPWT is used across numerous specialties, including dermatology, podiatry, plastic surgery, trauma, orthopedic surgery, general surgery, and vascular surgery, and can be applied in both inpatient and outpatient settings. Clear communication and coordination among team members are essential to optimize patient outcomes.
